newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Court awards disputed Belgrade to Milosevic.
newsitem.headline: Court awards disputed Belgrade to Milosevic.

text.p: Serbia's Supreme Court, in a decision that renewed three weeks of street protests, gave control of Belgrade city council to President Slobodan Milosevic on Sunday despite opposition charges of election rigging.

But the struggle for power between Milosevic's ruling socialists and the Zajedno (Together) coalition of opposition parties appeared unresolved after the city election commission submitted further appeals.

Opposition officials said Milosevic, under heavy U.S.-led Western pressure to honour democracy, could be trying to engineer a complete re-run of the November 17 local elections which have embroiled his nine-year reign in crisis.
More then 100,000 demonstrators, accusing the court of rubber-stamping socialist election fraud, thronged Belgrade on Sunday amid growing demands for Milosevic's removal.
In the southern industrial city of Nis, up to 50,000 people jammed the central square smashing a television set in protest against biased coverage by state-run media.
The court reversed the initial outcome of the elections and gave the socialists and their allies 66 of the 110 seats in the Belgrade city assembly.
Zajedno lawyer Goran Draganic said: "It is now clear to both the foreign and domestic public that what the Supreme Court did last night was founded on politics, not law."
With Zajedno promising to continue protests which have attracted up to 150,000 people day in Belgrade, opposition sources said Milosevic was trying to buy time for a face-saving solution.
The opposition's main fear is that he will choose force, as he did in 1991 when tanks were used to suppress the last major challenge to socialist supremacy.
Zajedno leader Vuk Draskovic told reporters: "I am expecting tomorrow, the day after tomorrow, that Milosevic will use police, maybe even the army, but we will not stop," he added.
Zajedno leaders are concerned that police provocateurs among the marchers could foment trouble and give Milosevic an excuse to turn loose his riot police.
Zajedno and Belgrade students staged separate marches on Sunday during which a wreath was laid at the door of Milosevic's office with the inscription: "Justice died here."
Draskovic compared Milosevic and his marxist wife Mirjana with Romanian dictator Nicolae Ceausescu and his wife who were overthrown and executed in 1989.

He told baying demonstrators: "We are not even the victims of a one-party dictatorship, but of a one-bed dictatorship. We are in the same position as Romania under the Ceausescus. There's only one objective now - resignation."
Mirjana, who leads her own United Yugoslav Left (YUL) party is even more unpopular than her husband with opposition supporters.

Aleksa Djilas, political analyst son of the late communist dissident Milovan Djilas, accused the opposition of being over-ambitious in trying to topple Milosevic and warned against relying on the West.

"I do not believe the West would support Milosevic's replacement because a successor is not in sight," Djilas told Beta news agency. "(The West) fears the nationalism of the opposition leaders and the anarchic situation in Serbia."
Draskovic accused Milosevic of ordering the Supreme Court to reject Zajedno appeals for the return of Belgrade city council seats it won.
Five of the 36 Supreme Court judges had earlier protested against the authorities' involvement of the judiciary in the settlement of a political conflict.

Radio B-92 reported that student Dejan Bulatovic suffered serious head and chest injuries when he was beaten by police after being arrested for carrying an effigy of Milosevic in prison garb during Saturday's demonstration.
